## Story

> Hallberg City Museum, Sunday night, ten past eleven, in the restoration lab in the basement. On the tables lie 2,400 clay fragments from the dig at Tell Varda, each with one sign of the Varda script, a script nobody has read yet. At 06:00 the crates are sealed and flown back to the excavation, and with them the Varda jar, whose lid carries six signs.
>
> Prof. Amara Okafor, who knows the script best, is stuck at the airport. Her notes, her student assistant's half-finished code and a laser scanner are all you have: teach a convolutional network to read the signs, and read the lid before the crates leave. Python here runs a TensorFlow-style model: a small library with TensorFlow's names (`import tensorflow as tf`), written for this room because the real TensorFlow can't run in a browser. The first puzzle you open takes a little while to load.

## Stations

### 1. The raking light

**Practises:** What a convolution computes: a sliding 3 × 3 window, point-by-point product and sum; how much smaller the result is; the same filter as a Keras Conv2D with set_weights; images with a channel axis  
**Needs:** 🔎 Theo's note, 🔎 Chart: Varda numerals  
**Data:** [tally.py](../../content/rooms/nn-tablets/data/tally.py)

**Task:**

> Theo's light table holds tablet V-17, a tally so worn that nobody can read it any more. The laser scanner measured its surface anyway: `scan`, the height of every point in millimetres. What number does it record?
>
> 1. Filter the scan by hand with a 3 × 3 kernel that makes worn signs visible: for every position, take the 3 × 3 window of `scan`, multiply it by the kernel point by point, and add it all up. Store the result as `edges`.
> 2. Do the same with Keras: `raking`, a model with one `Conv2D` layer (one 3 × 3 filter, no bias) and the same kernel loaded with `set_weights`. Check that `raking(scan[None, :, :, None])` gives your `edges`.
> 3. Look at `edges` with `show_images` and store the tally as `number`.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras import layers
from helpers import show_images

show_images(scan, title="Tablet V-17")
print(scan.shape)

kernel = None   # the 3 x 3 kernel, as a NumPy array
edges = None    # the scan filtered by hand: one number per 3 x 3 window
raking = None   # tf.keras.Sequential([...]) with one Conv2D layer, then set_weights
number = None   # the tally on the tablet
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras import layers
from helpers import show_images

kernel = np.array([[0, 1, 0], [1, -4, 1], [0, 1, 0]])
edges = np.array([[(scan[i:i + 3, j:j + 3] * kernel).sum() for j in range(94)] for i in range(28)])
show_images(edges, title="Tablet V-17 in raking light")

raking = tf.keras.Sequential([tf.keras.Input(shape=(30, 96, 1)), layers.Conv2D(1, 3, use_bias=False)])
raking.set_weights([kernel.reshape(3, 3, 1, 1)])
print(np.abs(raking(scan[None, :, :, None])[0, :, :, 0] - edges).max())
number = 246    # two bars, four circles, six wedges
```

**Checked result** (`_tally_check(edges, raking, number)`):

```json
"read"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> Tablet V-17 counts **246**: two hundreds, four tens and six ones.
>
> Theo's kernel compares every point with its four neighbours, so the tablet's gentle curve comes out as almost 0 and only the sharp dents light up. A `Conv2D` layer does exactly this: it slides a small kernel over the image and adds up products. A trained network learns its kernels itself.

**Hints:**

1. Theo, the restorer, left a note with the kernel. Two loops over the rows and columns of the result: `scan[i:i + 3, j:j + 3]` is the window at row `i`, column `j`. A 3 × 3 window fits 28 × 94 times into the 30 × 96 scan, so `edges` has the shape `(28, 94)`.
2. `(scan[i:i + 3, j:j + 3] * kernel).sum()` is one value. In Keras: `raking = tf.keras.Sequential([tf.keras.Input(shape=(30, 96, 1)), layers.Conv2D(1, 3, use_bias=False)])`. Its kernel has the shape `(3, 3, 1, 1)`: rows, columns, channels in, filters.
3. `edges = np.array([[(scan[i:i + 3, j:j + 3] * kernel).sum() for j in range(94)] for i in range(28)])`, then `raking.set_weights([kernel.reshape(3, 3, 1, 1)])`. Two tall bars, four circles, six wedges: `number = 246`.

### 2. The cylinder seal

**Practises:** A convolution as a search for a pattern; the kernel layout of Conv2D (rows, columns, channels in, filters); GlobalMaxPooling2D: the best match anywhere; scores and argmax  
**Needs:** 🔎 Amara's sign list, 🔎 The label in the glass case  
**Data:** [seal.py](../../content/rooms/nn-tablets/data/seal.py)

**Task:**

> In the glass case lies the only bilingual find from Tell Varda: a cylinder seal, rolled out on fresh clay. Its impression shows eight Varda signs side by side, `impressions`, one 24 × 24 depth scan each, and someone scratched their sounds below it. Which sound does each Varda sign stand for? Amara cut a stamp for each of the eight signs: `templates`, eight filters of 11 × 11.
>
> 1. Build `finder`, a Keras model that looks for every stamp anywhere in an impression: a `Conv2D` layer with 8 filters of 11 × 11 and no bias, then `GlobalMaxPooling2D`. Load the stamps as its filters: filter number `i` is `templates[i]`.
> 2. `finder.predict` gives 8 scores per impression, one per stamp. Store the sign number of each impression, left to right, as `order`.
> 3. Line the signs up with the sounds below them: `values`, a dict from every sign number (0 to 7) to its sound, e.g. `{0: "ba", ...}`.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras import layers
from helpers import show_images

show_images(impressions, labels=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], title="The seal's impression")
show_images(templates, labels=list(range(8)), title="Amara's stamps")
print(impressions.shape, templates.shape)

finder = None   # Conv2D with the 8 stamps as filters, then GlobalMaxPooling2D
order = None    # the sign number of each impression, left to right
values = None   # {sign number: sound}
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras import layers
from helpers import show_images

show_images(impressions, labels=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], title="The seal's impression")
finder = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.Input(shape=(24, 24, 1)),
    layers.Conv2D(8, 11, use_bias=False),
    layers.GlobalMaxPooling2D(),
])
finder.set_weights([templates.transpose(1, 2, 0)[:, :, None, :]])   # filter i = templates[i]
scores = finder.predict(impressions[..., None] / 255)
order = scores.argmax(axis=1).tolist()
print(order)

caption = ["lu", "ra", "sa", "ko", "ne", "re", "mi", "ta"]
values = dict(zip(order, caption))
print(values)
```

**Checked result** (`_seal_check(finder, order, values)`):

```json
"deciphered"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> The seal's signs are 5, 0, 7, 2, 6, 4, 1, 3, so the eight sounds are: 0 **ra** (sun), 1 **mi** (water), 2 **ko** (mountain), 3 **ta** (tree), 4 **re** (house), 5 **lu** (star), 6 **ne** (comb), 7 **sa** (eye).
>
> Your finder is a small convolutional network built by hand: each filter is a picture of what it looks for, the convolution scores every position, and global max pooling keeps the best score, wherever it was. A trained network works the same way, but it learns its filters, and they are smaller and stacked in layers.

**Hints:**

1. A Sequential model: `tf.keras.Input(shape=(24, 24, 1))`, `layers.Conv2D(8, 11, use_bias=False)`, `layers.GlobalMaxPooling2D()`. The Conv2D's kernel has the shape `(11, 11, 1, 8)`: rows, columns, channels in, filters. `templates` has the shape `(8, 11, 11)`: there the filters come first. The label in the glass case copies the scratched sounds.
2. `templates.reshape(11, 11, 1, 8)` has the right shape but scrambles the stamps. Move the axis instead: `templates.transpose(1, 2, 0)` has the shape `(11, 11, 8)`, and `[:, :, None, :]` adds the channel axis. The impressions need a channel axis too: `impressions[..., None]`.
3. `finder.set_weights([templates.transpose(1, 2, 0)[:, :, None, :]])`, then `order = finder.predict(impressions[..., None]).argmax(axis=1)` gives `[5, 0, 7, 2, 6, 4, 1, 3]`. With the caption: `values = {5: "lu", 0: "ra", 7: "sa", 2: "ko", 6: "ne", 4: "re", 1: "mi", 3: "ta"}`.

### 3. The stained blueprint

**Practises:** Output shapes of Conv2D and MaxPooling2D, valid vs. same padding, counting a convolution's parameters (kernel × kernel × channels in × filters + one bias per filter), GlobalMaxPooling2D vs. Flatten, summary()  
**Needs:** 🔎 Blueprint: the reader  
**Data:** [blueprint.py](../../content/rooms/nn-tablets/data/blueprint.py)

**Task:**

> Amara's blueprint for the reader hangs above the computer: draft 3, a small convolutional network. Someone put a coffee cup on it, and several numbers are gone.
>
> 1. Work out the missing pieces from what is still legible: the output shapes and the numbers of parameters.
> 2. Build draft 3 as a Keras model, `model`, so that `model.summary()` matches every number on the blueprint.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras import layers

model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.Input(shape=(24, 24, 1)),
    # ... the layers of draft 3
])
model.summary()
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras import layers

model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.Input(shape=(24, 24, 1)),
    layers.Conv2D(8, 3, padding="same", activation="relu"),   # 24 x 24 stays 24 x 24
    layers.MaxPooling2D(),                                     # 12 x 12
    layers.Conv2D(16, 3, activation="relu"),                   # (3 * 3 * 8 + 1) * 16 = 1,168
    layers.GlobalMaxPooling2D(),                               # (None, 16), no parameters
    layers.Dense(8, activation="softmax"),
])
model.summary()
```

**Checked result** (`_blueprint_check(model)`):

```json
"matches"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> Draft 3 has **1,384** parameters. The first Conv2D keeps the size with `padding="same"`, the second has 16 filters of 3 × 3 (3 · 3 · 8 · 16 + 16 = 1,168) and no padding, and the stain hid a `GlobalMaxPooling2D`: it keeps each filter's strongest response, wherever it was.
>
> A dense network with 64 neurons would need 37,448 parameters for the same 24 × 24 fragments. A convolution uses the same small kernel at every position.

**Hints:**

1. A Conv2D layer has kernel × kernel × channels in × filters weights, plus one bias per filter. A 3 × 3 kernel without padding makes the image 2 pixels smaller; `padding="same"` keeps its size. `MaxPooling2D()` halves it.
2. The first Conv2D stays at 24 × 24, so it has `padding="same"`. For the second, (k · k · 8 + 1) · 16 = 1,168 gives k = 3, and 12 → 10 means no padding. The stained layer turns `(None, 10, 10, 16)` into `(None, 16)` without parameters; Amara's margin note says which one.
3. `layers.Conv2D(8, 3, padding="same", activation="relu")`, `layers.MaxPooling2D()`, `layers.Conv2D(16, 3, activation="relu")`, `layers.GlobalMaxPooling2D()`, `layers.Dense(8, activation="softmax")`: 1,384 parameters.

**Model solution:**

```python
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras import layers

tf.keras.utils.set_random_seed(1)

model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.Input(shape=(24, 24, 1)),
    layers.Conv2D(8, 3, padding="same", activation="relu"),
    layers.MaxPooling2D(),
    layers.Conv2D(16, 3, activation="relu"),
    layers.GlobalMaxPooling2D(),
    layers.Dense(8, activation="softmax"),
])
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
history = model.fit(x_train[..., None] / 255, y_train, epochs=6, validation_split=0.2)

test_loss, test_accuracy = model.evaluate(x_test[..., None] / 255, y_test)
print("Test accuracy:", test_accuracy)

# Crate 7: where does the reader disagree with Mika's hand labels?
read = model.predict(x_crate[..., None] / 255).argmax(axis=1)
mika_wrong = int((read != y_mika).sum())
print("Mika got", mika_wrong, "wrong")
```

**Checked result** (`_notebook_check(model, mika_wrong)`):

```json
"trained"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> The reader reads about **95 %** of the test fragments. Mika made three mistakes: two poolings of 4 × 4 shrank the fragments to nothing (Keras says the output size would be negative), the fragments had no channel axis (Conv2D wants `(24, 24, 1)`, not `(24, 24)`), and after 2 epochs the reader was still learning. Here an epoch takes well under a second, so 6 to 8 are fine.
>
> On crate 7 the reader disagrees with Mika on **13** of the 60 fragments. A trained model can check hand labels: an archive sorted by hand always has some label noise.

**Hints:**

1. Read the first error: the second `MaxPooling2D` has nothing left to pool. Follow the shapes through the layers and compare them with the blueprint; `model.summary()` shows them once the model builds.
2. Conv2D wants every fragment with a channel axis: `(24, 24, 1)`, not `(24, 24)`. `x_train[..., None]` adds it, and `x_test` needs it too. Then look at the accuracy after the last epoch: is it still climbing? For crate 7, prepare `x_crate` the same way, let the reader predict, and compare with `y_mika`.
3. The layers from the blueprint, then `model.fit(x_train[..., None] / 255, y_train, epochs=6, validation_split=0.2)` and `model.evaluate(x_test[..., None] / 255, y_test)`. For crate 7: `read = model.predict(x_crate[..., None] / 255).argmax(axis=1)` and `mika_wrong = int((read != y_mika).sum())`.

### 5. Amara's laptop

**Practises:** Evaluating models with predict, argmax and a count; why a dense network is tied to pixel positions; translation invariance from convolution and global pooling; np.roll  
**Needs:** 🔒 1. The raking light, 🔎 Amara's mail, printed out  
**Data:** [laptop.py](../../content/rooms/nn-tablets/data/laptop.py)

**Code lock** (opens with `246`):

> Amara's laptop asks for a password. On the lid, in her handwriting: "The first tablet I ever read: the tally on V-17."

**Task:**

> Amara's laptop holds her old reader, `old_reader`, a dense network, and `prototype`, a first try of draft 3. Both learned from the dig's photo set, where every sign sits in the middle of its fragment. The 100 fragments that came in last week, `x_new` with their sign numbers `y_new`, have their signs anywhere. Which reader copes with that, and why does the other one fail?
>
> 1. How many of the 100 new fragments does each reader read right? Store the counts as `old_right` and `proto_right`. Prepare the fragments the way the readers expect them.
> 2. Test both readers on `probe`, a fragment with a star (5) in the middle: shift it 0, 1, 2, ... pixels to the right with `np.roll(probe, shift, axis=1)` and plot each reader's probability for the star. `first_miss`: the smallest shift at which the old reader no longer reads a star.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
import numpy as np
from helpers import show_images, show_plot

old_reader.summary()
prototype.summary()
show_images(x_new[:10], labels=list(y_new[:10]), title="New fragments")

old_right = None     # how many of the 100 new fragments the old reader reads right
proto_right = None   # ... and the prototype
first_miss = None    # the smallest shift at which the old reader misses the star
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
import numpy as np
from helpers import show_images, show_plot

x = x_new[..., None] / 255
old_right = int((old_reader.predict(x).argmax(axis=1) == y_new).sum())
proto_right = int((prototype.predict(x).argmax(axis=1) == y_new).sum())
print(old_right, proto_right)

shifted = np.stack([np.roll(probe, s, axis=1) for s in range(9)])[..., None] / 255
old_probs, proto_probs = old_reader.predict(shifted), prototype.predict(shifted)
show_plot(old_probs[:, 5], proto_probs[:, 5], labels=["old reader", "prototype"], title="Probability of a star, shifted to the right")
first_miss = int(np.flatnonzero(old_probs.argmax(axis=1) != 5)[0])
print(first_miss)
```

**Checked result** (`_laptop_check(old_right, proto_right, first_miss)`):

```json
"compared"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> The old reader gets **18** of the 100 new fragments right, little better than guessing; the prototype gets **98**. Move the star 3 pixels and the old reader loses it: a dense layer has one weight per pixel, so it learned where a star's strokes lie, not what a star looks like. The prototype's filters slide over the whole fragment, and global max pooling keeps their best match wherever it is.

**Hints:**

1. Both readers expect `(n, 24, 24, 1)` with values from 0.0 to 1.0: `x_new[..., None] / 255`. `predict` gives 8 probabilities per fragment, `.argmax(axis=1)` the sign; compare with `y_new` and count with `.sum()`.
2. `shifted = np.stack([np.roll(probe, s, axis=1) for s in range(9)])`, prepared the same way. Column 5 of `old_reader.predict(...)` is the old reader's probability for the star at each shift; `show_plot` draws both readers' lines.
3. `old_right = 18`, `proto_right = 98`, `first_miss = 3`.

**Task:**

> The lid of the Varda jar carries six signs in a scribe's hand: `jar`, a depth scan of 24 rows × 144 columns, one sign in each 24 × 24 field. The crates leave at 06:00. What does the lid say?
>
> 1. Train the reader on the archive. It needs at least 85 % on the test fragments.
> 2. Cut the lid into its six fields and prepare them for the reader: `fragments`. Let the reader read them: `signs`, the six sign numbers from left to right.
> 3. `word`: how the lid sounds, one syllable per sign, e.g. `"ba-de-fo-gu-hi-jo"`.

**Model solution:**

```python
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras import layers
from helpers import show_images

tf.keras.utils.set_random_seed(1)
show_images(jar, title="The jar's lid")

model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.Input(shape=(24, 24, 1)),
    layers.Conv2D(8, 3, padding="same", activation="relu"),
    layers.MaxPooling2D(),
    layers.Conv2D(16, 3, activation="relu"),
    layers.GlobalMaxPooling2D(),
    layers.Dense(8, activation="softmax"),
])
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
history = model.fit(x_train[..., None] / 255, y_train, epochs=6, validation_split=0.2)
print(model.evaluate(x_test[..., None] / 255, y_test))

fragments = np.stack(np.hsplit(jar, 6))[..., None] / 255
signs = model.predict(fragments).argmax(axis=1).tolist()
values = {0: "ra", 1: "mi", 2: "ko", 3: "ta", 4: "re", 5: "lu", 6: "ne", 7: "sa"}   # from the seal
word = "-".join(values[s] for s in signs)
print(signs, word)
```

**Checked result** (`_jar_check(model, fragments, signs, word)`):

```json
"read"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> The reader reads the lid: **ta-lu-mi-ra-ko-ne**. At 05:52 you send it to Amara, and her answer comes from the airport: "Talumi Rakone. A name, the potter who made the jar or the one who owned it. It's the first word anyone has read in the Varda script in three thousand years."
>
> Your reader learned eight signs from 2,400 fragments with 1,384 parameters, because a convolution looks for the same small shapes everywhere, and global pooling doesn't care where it found them.

**Hints:**

1. The reader is the fixed notebook's model, trained the same way. The lid is six 24 × 24 fields side by side: `np.hsplit(jar, 6)` cuts it, and `np.stack(...)` makes one array of shape `(6, 24, 24)`.
2. Prepare the fields exactly like `x_train`: channel axis and `/ 255`. `model.predict(fragments).argmax(axis=1)` gives the sign numbers; the seal's reveal gives the sound of each number.
3. `fragments = np.stack(np.hsplit(jar, 6))[..., None] / 255`. The signs are `[3, 5, 1, 0, 2, 6]`, the word is `"ta-lu-mi-ra-ko-ne"`.

## Clues in the room

### 🔎 Theo's note

*Used by: 1. The raking light*

> Raking light, the digital way (T. Brandt, restorer)
>
> Worn signs are dents a few hundredths of a millimetre deep, on a tablet that curves by several millimetres. To see them, compare every point with its four neighbours, using this 3 × 3 kernel:
>
> `0   1   0`
> `1  -4   1`
> `0   1   0`
>
> Smooth curves come out close to 0; sharp dents light up.

### 🔎 Chart: Varda numerals

> HOW THE VARDA SCRIBES COUNTED
>
> A tall bar: one hundred
> A circle: ten
> A wedge (a small triangle): one
>
> The scribes pressed as many of each as they needed, hundreds first. Add them up.

### 🔎 The label on the crates

*Used by: 4. Mika's notebook, 6. The Varda jar*

> VARDA ARCHIVE · fragments, signs sorted by hand
>
> 2,400 fragments to learn from (`x_train`, `y_train`) and 600 to test with (`x_test`, `y_test`).
>
> Every fragment is a depth scan of 24 × 24 points, stored as bytes: **0 = the clay's surface, 255 = deepest**. One sign on each, anywhere. Labels: the sign's number from the sign list, 0 to 7.
>
> The reader wants every point from 0.0 to 1.0.

**Images as arrays:** [`a[i:i + 3, j:j + 3]`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/basics.indexing.html), [`x[..., None]`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/basics.indexing.html#dimensional-indexing-tools), [`a.transpose(axes)`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.transpose.html), [`np.hsplit(a, n)  np.stack(arrays)`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.hsplit.html), [`np.roll(a, shift, axis)`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.roll.html), `show_images(images, labels=None, title=None)`, `show_plot(*series, labels=None, title=None)`

**Convolution:** [`layers.Conv2D(filters, kernel_size, padding="valid", activation=None, use_bias=True)`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/layers/Conv2D), [`images: (samples, rows, columns, channels)`](https://www.tensorflow.org/tutorials/images/cnn), [`padding="valid"  padding="same"`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/layers/Conv2D), [`Conv2D parameters`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/layers/Conv2D), [`set_weights([kernel])`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/Model#set_weights)

**Pooling:** [`layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=2)`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/layers/MaxPool2D), [`layers.GlobalMaxPooling2D()`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/layers/GlobalMaxPool2D), [`layers.Flatten()`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/layers/Flatten)

**Building and training:** [`tf.keras.Sequential([...])  model.summary()`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/Sequential), [`layers.Dense(units, activation="softmax")`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/layers/Dense), [`model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/Model#compile), [`model.fit(x, y, epochs, validation_split)`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/Model#fit), [`model.evaluate(x, y)  model.predict(x)`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/Model#predict), [`tf.keras.utils.set_random_seed(n)`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/utils/set_random_seed)
